people.name: Quintilian
people.summary: Rhetorician from Calagurris in Spain, first holder of the state chair of Latin rhetoric founded by Vespasian, and author of the twelve-book Institutio Oratoria, the most complete ancient treatise on education and oratory.
people.detail: Brought to Rome by Galba in 68, he taught for twenty years (Pliny the Younger was a pupil), retired c. 90 and was given consular ornaments for tutoring the sons of Flavius Clemens. He lost his young wife and two sons, grief he records in the preface to Book 6.

people.name: Statius
people.summary: Neapolitan poet of Domitian's court, author of the epic Thebaid, the unfinished Achilleid and the Silvae, occasional poems on court life, villas and friends.
people.detail: His father was a famous teacher and poet at Naples. Statius won at Domitian's Alban games but lost at the Capitoline, and retired to Naples. Dante made him a guide in Purgatorio.

people.name: Juvenal
people.summary: Satirist whose sixteen verse Satires, published c. 110-130, are the fiercest Roman portraits of urban life, social injustice and vice.
people.detail: Martial addresses him as a friend toiling through the clients' round. An inscription from Aquinum may name him as a militia officer, and the ancient Lives claim he was exiled to Egypt for mocking an actor, details of doubtful value.

people.name: Suetonius
people.summary: Biographer and imperial secretary, protege of Pliny the Younger, author of the Lives of the Twelve Caesars and of lives of grammarians, rhetoricians and poets; dismissed by Hadrian in 122 for overfamiliarity with Sabina.
people.detail: Pliny obtained for him the ius trium liberorum. An inscription from Hippo Regius lists his court posts. His lost works included treatises on games, courtesans, Greek insults and the Roman year.

people.name: Plutarch
people.summary: Platonist philosopher and biographer from Chaeronea in Boeotia, priest at Delphi for some thirty years, author of the Parallel Lives and the Moralia.
people.detail: He studied at Athens under Ammonius, visited Rome and Alexandria and lectured in Rome under Vespasian or Domitian. His Roman citizenship came through Lucius Mestrius Florus. His works, some 78 essays and 50 lives surviving, shaped the European image of antiquity.

people.name: Clement of Rome
people.summary: Leading presbyter of the Roman church in the 90s, traditionally its third or fourth bishop, to whom the letter of the Roman church to the Corinthians (1 Clement, c. 96) is attributed.
people.detail: Later legend identified him with the consul Flavius Clemens and made him a martyr in the Crimea; a mass of pseudo-Clementine literature (Homilies, Recognitions) grew up around his name. The basilica of San Clemente in Rome is built over a house and mithraeum associated with him.
people.death: unknown (later legend: martyred in the Chersonese)

people.name: Ignatius of Antioch
people.summary: Bishop of Antioch condemned under Trajan and taken to Rome for the beasts, writing on the journey seven letters that are the earliest witness to the single bishop as head of each church and the first use of "catholic church".
people.detail: He met Polycarp at Smyrna; his letter to the Romans begs them not to save him. Origen and Eusebius say he was Peter's second successor at Antioch.
people.death: thrown to the beasts in Rome, c. 107-115

people.name: Polycarp
people.summary: Bishop of Smyrna for some fifty years, linked by Irenaeus to John and the apostles, recipient of a letter from Ignatius and author of a letter to the Philippians; burned at Smyrna aged 86, probably in 155-156.
people.detail: He visited Anicetus of Rome to discuss the Easter date. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, a letter of the Smyrnaean church, is the oldest martyr narrative outside the New Testament; he told the proconsul "86 years I have served him and he has done me no wrong".

people.name: Marcion
people.summary: Wealthy shipowner from Sinope who taught at Rome that the God of the Jewish scriptures was a lesser, just creator distinct from the good Father revealed by Jesus, and compiled the first Christian canon (a version of Luke and ten Pauline letters); expelled by the Roman church c. 144.
people.detail: He returned a donation of 200,000 sesterces on his expulsion. His church spread widely and survived in Syria into the fifth century. Tertullian's five books Against Marcion preserve much of his Antitheses.

people.name: Valentinus
people.summary: Egyptian-born Christian teacher active at Rome c. 136-160 whose mythological theology of aeons and the fallen Sophia founded the most important Gnostic school, the Valentinians.
people.detail: Educated in Alexandria, he reportedly claimed instruction from Theudas, a disciple of Paul. Tertullian says he expected to be bishop. Fragments survive in Clement of Alexandria, and the Gospel of Truth may be his.

people.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
people.summary: Bishop of Lyon after the persecution of 177, a native of Asia who had heard Polycarp, author of Against Heresies (c. 180), the foundational statement of apostolic succession and the four-gospel canon.
people.detail: He carried the Lyon confessors' letter to Rome and mediated in the Easter controversy. His Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching survives in Armenian. Later tradition, not early, makes him a martyr.

people.name: Montanus
people.summary: Phrygian convert who with the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla launched the ecstatic "New Prophecy" c. 156-172, announcing the age of the Paraclete and the descent of the new Jerusalem at Pepuza.
people.detail: Opponents claimed he had been a priest of Cybele and that he and Maximilla hanged themselves, hostile stories. His movement attracted Tertullian and persisted for centuries.

people.name: Victor I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome c. 189-199, an African and the first Latin-speaking holder of the see, who tried to impose Sunday Easter on the churches of Asia and gave Marcia the list of confessors in the Sardinian mines.
people.detail: Jerome credits him with the first Latin theological works. He excommunicated the adoptionist Theodotus the Cobbler.

people.name: Callistus

roles.t: Deacon in charge of the cemetery

people.summary: Former slave of an imperial freedman, condemned to the Sardinian mines and freed through Marcia c. 190, who became deacon in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Via Appia (the Catacomb of Callistus) and bishop of Rome 217-222.
people.detail: Hippolytus, his rival, accuses him of banking fraud and laxity in readmitting sinners. He may have died in a riot in Trastevere.

people.name: Fronto

roles.t: Tutor of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus

people.summary: Orator from Cirta in Numidia, the leading Latin rhetorician of the Antonine age, tutor and lifelong correspondent of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, consul in 143.
people.detail: His letters, recovered from palimpsests in the nineteenth century, reveal court life and his disappointment at Marcus's turn to philosophy. He was in poor health with gout for most of his life and seems to have died of the plague c. 167.

people.name: Apuleius

roles.t: Priest of the provincial cult of Africa

people.summary: Platonist philosopher, orator and novelist from Madauros in Numidia, author of the Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), the only complete surviving Latin novel, and of the Apology, his defence against charges of magic at Sabratha.
people.detail: Educated at Carthage, Athens and Rome, initiated into several mystery cults, he became a celebrated lecturer at Carthage. Augustine, also from Madauros, discussed his demonology.

people.name: Lucian of Samosata
people.summary: Syrian-born Greek satirist and sophist whose some 80 works mock philosophers, frauds, historians, the gods and the credulous, among them How to Write History, True Histories and Alexander the False Prophet.
people.detail: He gave up a career as a sculptor for rhetoric, toured Ionia, Italy and Gaul, settled at Athens and late in life took a salaried post in the prefect of Egypt's administration.

people.name: Pausanias
people.summary: Greek traveller from Lydia whose ten-book Description of Greece (c. 155-180), concentrating on sanctuaries, monuments, art and local myth, is the basic guide for the archaeology of mainland Greece.
people.detail: He mentions Herodes Atticus's Odeion and the Costoboci raid of 170. Little else is known of him.

people.name: Appian

roles.t: Advocate of the fisc and procurator

people.summary: Alexandrian Greek who practised law at Rome, received a procuratorship through Fronto under Antoninus Pius and wrote a Roman History arranged by peoples and wars, including five books on the Civil Wars.
people.detail: He experienced the Jewish revolt in Egypt (116-117) and narrowly escaped. His Civil Wars is the main continuous narrative of 133-35 BC.

people.name: Celsus
people.summary: Platonist author of the True Doctrine (Alethes Logos, c. 175-180), the first known systematic philosophical attack on Christianity, preserved through Origen's reply Contra Celsum.
people.detail: Origen confused him with an Epicurean of the same name; his identity and place are unknown.

people.name: Alexander of Abonoteichus
people.summary: Paphlagonian founder of the oracle of the snake god Glykon at Abonoteichus, which attracted Roman senators and an oracle request from Marcus Aurelius; Lucian's hostile Alexander the False Prophet exposes his tricks.
people.detail: He persuaded the emperor to rename his town Ionopolis and married his daughter to the consular Rutilianus. Statues and coins of Glykon show the cult's reach from the Danube to Athens.
people.death: gangrene of the leg (Lucian), aged nearly 70

people.name: Julia Balbilla
people.summary: Greek poet and companion of the empress Sabina, granddaughter of Antiochus IV of Commagene, who carved four epigrams in Aeolic Greek on the Colossus of Memnon during the imperial visit of November 130.
people.detail: Her brother was Philopappus, whose monument stands on the Hill of the Muses at Athens. The epigrams are among the very few surviving poems by Roman women.

sources.w: Les inscriptions grecques et latines du Colosse de Memnon (Bernand)

people.name: Tarrutenius Paternus
people.summary: Equestrian officer and military jurist (author of De re militari) who served Marcus as secretary and praetorian prefect, won the last great battle against the Quadi in 179, and was executed by Commodus in 182 after the Lucilla conspiracy, having been elevated to the Senate to remove him from the prefecture.
people.detail: Dio says he negotiated with the Cotini during the war. Fragments of his military law survive in the Digest.

people.name: Junius Rusticus
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, grandson of the Arulenus Rusticus executed by Domitian, Marcus Aurelius's most valued teacher, who introduced him to Epictetus; as urban prefect he condemned Justin Martyr c. 165.
people.detail: Marcus thanks him in Meditations 1.7 for showing him the need to correct his character and for lending him his copy of Epictetus. He was consul a second time in 162, a rare honour.

people.name: Sohaemus
people.fullName: Gaius Julius Sohaemus, King of Armenia
people.summary: Prince of the Emesene and Arsacid lines, a Roman senator and consul, who was installed as king of Armenia by Lucius Verus in 164 at the new capital Kainepolis, expelled c. 172 and restored by Martius Verus.
people.detail: The novelist Iamblichus claimed he knew him. Coins of Verus show the investiture with the legend REX ARMENIIS DATVS.

people.name: Ariogaesus
people.summary: Elected king by the Quadi in 174 after they expelled the Roman nominee Furtius; Marcus put a price on his head and, when he was captured, exiled him to Alexandria.
people.detail: His case shows Rome claiming the right to approve the rulers of the Quadi, as Antoninus's REX QVADIS DATVS coins advertised.

people.name: Aufidius Victorinus
people.summary: Fronto's son-in-law and Marcus's fellow student, who repelled the Chatti from Upper Germany in 162, governed Dacia and the Spanish provinces, and as urban prefect under Commodus was the most respected senator of his day; he was consul again with Commodus in 183.
people.detail: Dio says he faced down Perennis and died, possibly by suicide, around 185.

people.name: Pompeius Falco
people.summary: Trajanic and Hadrianic general who governed Judaea, Lower Moesia and Britain, where he restored order after the unrest at Hadrian's accession, before Platorius Nepos took over and built the Wall; correspondent of Pliny the Younger.
people.detail: He married the granddaughter of Sosius Senecio and is said to have shown Fronto his vine-grafting experiments.

people.name: Gnaeus Julius Verus
people.summary: Son of Sextus Julius Severus, governor of Britain c. 155-158, who brought reinforcements from Germany after trouble in the north and began the recommissioning of Hadrian's Wall; later legate of Syria in the Parthian war.
people.detail: He was designated for a second consulship c. 180 but died before holding it.

people.name: Terentius Scaurianus
people.summary: First consular governor of the province of Dacia (c. 106-110), founder of the colony Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa according to its foundation inscription.
people.detail: He had commanded in the Second Dacian War; military diplomas of 109-110 name him.

people.name: Abgar VII
people.fullName: Abgar VII bar Ezad, King of Osroene
people.summary: King of Edessa who submitted to Trajan in 114-115, winning favour through his son Arbandes, but joined the Mesopotamian revolt of 116 and was killed when Lusius Quietus sacked Edessa.
people.detail: After his death Osroene was briefly administered directly, then given to the Parthian prince Parthamaspates.

people.name: Valerius Asiaticus
people.summary: Senator from Vienna in Narbonensis, the first Gaul to hold two consulships, a ringleader in the murder of Caligula, who owned the Gardens of Lucullus and was destroyed by Messalina's intrigue in 47.
people.detail: He had accompanied Claudius to Britain. After Caligula's murder he told the crowd he wished he had done it.

people.name: Opramoas of Rhodiapolis
people.summary: Lycian millionaire whose tomb at Rhodiapolis carries some seventy letters from Antoninus Pius, governors and the Lycian League honouring his donations of over 500,000 denarii to cities rebuilding after the earthquake of c. 141.
people.detail: The dossier is a key document of provincial euergetism and of the way imperial honours were negotiated through letters.

people.name: Ummidius Quadratus
people.summary: Long-serving governor of Syria (c. 51-60) who failed to prevent Radamistus's seizure of Armenia, adjudicated the Samaritan-Jewish conflict under Cumanus, and quarrelled with Corbulo over the eastern command.
people.detail: His career inscription from Casinum records service under Tiberius. He died in office.

people.name: Septicius Clarus
people.summary: Friend of Pliny the Younger, to whom Pliny dedicated his letters, and of Suetonius, who dedicated the Lives of the Caesars to him; praetorian prefect from 119, dismissed with Suetonius in 122.
people.detail: The Historia Augusta says the cause was their behaviour toward Sabina without the emperor's permission.

people.name: Crispina
people.summary: Daughter of the consular Bruttius Praesens, married to Commodus in 178 before the second German expedition; accused of adultery, she was exiled to Capri c. 182 or later and put to death.
people.detail: Her coins show Venus, Juno Lucina and Concordia. Her disgrace has been placed in 182 after the Lucilla conspiracy or as late as 187-188.

people.name: Milonia Caesonia
people.summary: Fourth wife of Caligula, older than he and already mother of three daughters, whom he married in 39 when she bore him a daughter, Julia Drusilla; she and the child were killed immediately after his assassination.
people.detail: Suetonius reports he displayed her naked to friends and rode with her in military cloak; rumour said she drove him mad with a love potion.
people.death: killed by a centurion with her daughter, January 41

people.name: Statilia Messalina
people.summary: Third wife of Nero, married in 66 after Nero forced her husband Atticus Vestinus to suicide; a highly educated woman who survived Nero and was courted by Otho in 69.
people.detail: Inscriptions record her at the Vatican and among the Arval Brethren's honours. Otho's last letters were addressed to her.

people.name: Matidia the Elder
people.summary: Daughter of Trajan's sister Marciana, mother of Hadrian's wife Sabina, named Augusta in 112; Hadrian deified her on her death in 119, delivered her funeral oration and built a temple to her in the Campus Martius, the first temple to a deified mother-in-law.
people.detail: Fragments of Hadrian's laudatio survive on an inscription from Tibur. She accompanied Trajan to the East and returned with his ashes.

people.name: Marciana
people.summary: Elder sister of Trajan, made Augusta c. 105, mother of Matidia and grandmother of Sabina; she lived in harmony with Plotina in the palace and was deified on her death in 112, when Matidia succeeded to her title.
people.detail: Trajan named the colony Marcianopolis in Moesia and the Thamugadi foundation (Colonia Marciana Traiana Thamugadi) after her.

people.name: Domitia Lucilla
people.summary: Mother of Marcus Aurelius, heiress of an immense fortune including brickworks near Rome, a cultivated woman whose house was a centre of Greek culture; Marcus thanks her in the Meditations for her piety, generosity and simple living.
people.detail: The Domitian brickyards she owned passed to Marcus and became imperial property, their stamps a dating tool for Roman buildings. Fronto's letters show the young Marcus chatting with her at Antoninus's villas.

people.name: Julia Titi
people.summary: Daughter of Titus, given the title Augusta, who after her husband Flavius Sabinus was executed lived openly with her uncle Domitian; her death in 91, rumoured to have followed an abortion he forced on her, was followed by her deification.
people.detail: Her portraits with towering curls are a hallmark of Flavian female fashion; she appears on coins as DIVA IVLIA.

people.name: Furius Victorinus
people.summary: Equestrian prefect of Egypt and praetorian prefect from 159, who accompanied Lucius Verus to the East and died of plague with part of his army on the northern front in 168.
people.detail: His death is recorded by the Historia Augusta. He was succeeded by Macrinius Vindex, killed in battle with the Marcomanni in 170.

people.name: Claudius Severus
people.summary: First governor of the province of Arabia (c. 107-115), builder of the Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to Aila, whose name appears on its milestones; a letter of a soldier named Julius Apollinaris on papyrus mentions him.
people.detail: His family produced Marcus Aurelius's Peripatetic friend Claudius Severus Arabianus and Commodus's brother-in-law.

people.name: Anicetus
people.summary: Bishop of Rome c. 155-166, from Emesa according to the Liber Pontificalis, who received Polycarp of Smyrna and agreed to differ with him on the date of Easter.
people.detail: Hegesippus visited Rome in his time and compiled a succession list of Roman bishops.
